sections.b: No book of the Greek Old Testament praises almsgiving more than Tobit. Tobit's memoir begins with the alms he gave in exile (Tobit 1:3, 16–17), Anna mocks him with them (Tobit 2:14), and his charge to his son makes them the heart of the faithful life: give from what you have, much or little; you store up a good deposit for the day of need; "alms rescue from death and do not let a person go into the darkness" (Tobit 4:7–11, from the shorter Greek text). The book reads Proverbs' "righteousness rescues from death" (Proverbs 10:2; Proverbs 11:4) with tsedaqah in its later sense of charity. Early Christians quoted it (Polycarp, Philippians 10:2; Cyprian, On Works and Alms), and at the Reformation the verse became a point of dispute between Catholics and Lutherans over whether good works take away sin.

common: Tobit is the classic Jewish text for almsgiving as a central religious duty, alongside Sirach 3:30 and 29:8–13.
uncommon: Some scholars think Tobit's "death" in 4:10 means an untimely death in this life, not judgment after death, which would narrow the later Catholic-Protestant dispute.

sections.h: Tobit, the man who buried the dead
sections.b: Tobit's chief good work is burying Israelites whose bodies the Assyrian kings threw outside Nineveh's wall (Tobit 1:17–19). It costs him his property and nearly his life, and at Pentecost he leaves his dinner untasted to bury a murdered man (Tobit 2:3–8). He asks his son to bury him and his wife well (Tobit 4:3–4), and Tobias's fear is that no son will be left to bury his parents (Tobit 6:15). The waiting until sunset and the washing (Tobit 2:4–5) reflect the law's rules on corpses (Numbers 19:11–13; Deuteronomy 21:23). Christian teaching later added burying the dead to the six works of mercy of Matthew 25, and Thomas Aquinas praised Tobias's example (Summa II-II q.32 a.2, ad 1).

sections.h: Raphael, the angel who travels with Tobias
sections.b: In Tobit God answers two prayers by sending Raphael, "God heals" (Tobit 3:16–17). He appears as a young Israelite, Azariah, hired as a guide (Tobit 5:4–16), and Tobit, not knowing, prays that God's angel will go with the travelers (Tobit 5:17) and assures Anna that "a good angel will go with him" (Tobit 5:22). The story is the fullest picture before the New Testament of an angel as a personal companion and protector, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching on guardian angels draws on it alongside Psalm 91:11 and Matthew 18:10. The 66 books name only Michael and Gabriel.

common: Raphael is counted with Michael and Gabriel as an archangel in Catholic and Orthodox worship.

sections.b: Tobit's demon Asmodeus kills each of Sarah's seven husbands on the wedding night (Tobit 3:8; Tobit 6:14–15). His name probably comes from Persian aēšma-daēva, "demon of wrath." Raphael is sent to free Sarah from him (Tobit 3:17) and teaches Tobias to drive him off with smoke and prayer (Tobit 6:8, 17–18). In later Jewish tradition he is Ashmedai, king of the demons (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 68a–b).

sections.h: Demon and evil spirit in Tobit
sections.b: Tobit uses the Gospels' words, daimonion and pneuma ponēron, for a spirit that attacks people (Tobit 6:8). Unlike Saul's "evil spirit from God" (1 Samuel 16:14), this one is God's enemy, defeated by the angel God sends. The remedy is smoke from a fish's heart and liver with prayer, a means no book of the 66 uses: Jesus drives out spirits with a word (Mark 1:25; Matthew 8:16).

Tobit is the story of a family from the northern tribe of Naphtali, carried to Nineveh by Assyria (Tobit 1:1–3), with kinsmen in the towns of Media (Tobit 1:14; compare 2 Kings 17:6). It imagines how the northern exiles lived and kept faith, and ends with a hope that all Israel will be gathered (Tobit 13–14).

Tobit sets its story in Nineveh under Shalmaneser (Greek "Enemessar"), Sennacherib and Esarhaddon (Tobit 1:2, 15, 21). It agrees with Kings on Sennacherib's failed campaign against Judah and his murder by his sons (Tobit 1:18, 21; 2 Kings 19:35–37), but compresses twenty years into forty days and makes Sennacherib Shalmaneser's son, leaving out Sargon II. Its picture of a Jew rising at the Assyrian court borrows the figure of Ahiqar, Esarhaddon's legendary wise counselor.

Tobit 1:6–8 is one of the earliest witnesses to the Jewish reading of the law as requiring three tithes: a first tithe to the Levites (Numbers 18:21), a second tithe eaten in Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 14:22–26), and every third year a tithe for orphans, widows and converts (Deuteronomy 14:28–29; Deuteronomy 26:12). Josephus knows all three (Antiquities 4.240); Jubilees 32 knows the second tithe.

In Nineveh Tobit's kinsmen "ate the food of the Gentiles," but he did not (Tobit 1:10–11), like Daniel (Daniel 1:8) and Judith (Judith 12:1–4). The law bans unclean animals and blood, not Gentile bread; avoiding Gentile food was a later widening, the background of Acts 10:14 and Acts 11:3.

sections.h: The calf at Dan in Tobit
sections.b: Tobit says all his tribe sacrificed "to the calf that Jeroboam king of Israel had made in Dan" (Tobit 1:5), the shrine nearest Naphtali (1 Kings 12:29). The shorter Greek text calls it "Baal the heifer."

Tobit tells his son to take a wife from his father's tribe, as Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob did (Tobit 4:12–13), and the plot brings Tobias to his kinswoman Sarah, "allotted to you before the ages" (Tobit 6:18). The book stretches the rule for heiresses (Numbers 36:6–9) into an ideal for exiles threatened with assimilation. Raphael's counsel to pray before the wedding night (Tobit 6:18), expanded in the Vulgate into three nights of prayer (Vulgate Tobit 6:16–22), shaped centuries of Christian teaching on marriage.

sections.h: "Do not do to anyone what you hate" (Tobit 4:15)
sections.b: Tobit 4:15, which survives in Greek only in the shorter text (Vaticanus and Alexandrinus) because Sinaiticus has a gap there, is the oldest surviving Jewish form of the Golden Rule, in the negative: do not do to others what you hate. Hillel gave it the same way (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a), and so does the Didache (1:2). Jesus states it positively (Matthew 7:12; Luke 6:31).

Tobit makes Ahiqar, the wise counselor of the famous Aramaic Story of Ahiqar, his own nephew (Tobit 1:21–22; Tobit 2:10), and Tobit's charge to his son (Tobit 4:3–21) is a wisdom instruction like Proverbs 1–9, close in form to Ahiqar's sayings.

Tobit 3 sets two prayers side by side: Tobit's confession that God is just and the exile deserved (Tobit 3:2–6), and Sarah's blessing and plea at her window (Tobit 3:11–15). Both ask for death, and both are heard at the same moment (Tobit 3:16). Tobit's prayer follows the pattern of Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9 and Daniel 9; Sarah's opens with "Blessed are you," the form of later Jewish blessings.

Taunted over the deaths of seven husbands, Sarah goes up to hang herself, then stops: her father would be shamed and brought down to the grave in grief. She prays instead (Tobit 3:10–15). It is one of the few ancient Jewish scenes of someone choosing against suicide.

Tobit is blinded while doing good, loses his income, and is mocked by his wife: "Where are your alms now?" (Tobit 2:10–14), as Job's wife mocks him (Job 2:9). He asks to die (Tobit 3:6). Unlike Job, Tobit confesses his sins, and the story answers with healing through an angel. Jerome's Latin makes the comparison with Job explicit (Vulgate Tobit 2:12–18).

sections.h: Hades and "the everlasting place" in Tobit
sections.b: Tobit's Greek calls the realm of the dead Hades (Tobit 3:10; Tobit 4:19), as the Septuagint renders Sheol, and speaks of "the darkness" (Tobit 4:10) and "the everlasting place" (Tobit 3:6). Sarah's fear of bringing her father down to Hades in sorrow echoes Jacob (Genesis 42:38).

In Tobit God works without miracles that anyone sees. Two prayers on one day are answered by one angel (Tobit 3:16–17); the help comes as a hired guide no one recognizes (Tobit 5:4); a fish's organs become the cure; and a bride is "allotted" from before the ages (Tobit 6:18). The reader is told from the start what the characters must learn by trusting.
Tobit 2:1 calls the Feast of Weeks "Pentecost," one of the earliest uses of the Greek name, and shows a family keeping it far from the temple with a feast shared with the poor (Deuteronomy 16:11).

Tobit is a story of the diaspora. Its hero keeps the law in Nineveh, confesses that the exile is the covenant curse coming true ("you made us a proverb... among all the nations where you scattered us," Tobit 3:4; compare Deuteronomy 28:37), and finds that God has not forgotten his scattered people.
